descriptionChirho: The core Qal active sense with a female subject meaning 'to bear, give birth to a child.' Arabic وَلَدَتْ (waladat) consistently marks feminine active birthing; Korean 낳다 (nahda) 'to give birth' is uniform across all these clusters; Swahili uses -zaa (active birthing, e.g., alizaa, akazaa, alimzaa, alimzalia with applicative). This covers all Qal perfects, imperfects, infinitives, and waw-consecutives with feminine subjects, including participial forms meaning 'one who bears / woman in labor' (Arabic الْوَالِدَة al-waalida; Korean 해산하는 여인 haesanhaneun yeoin; Swahili mzazi, anayezaa).

The Qal active sense with a male subject meaning 'to beget, to father.' Arabic وَلَدَ (walada) with masculine conjugation; English consistently uses 'fathered, begot, begat'; Spanish engendro; Korean 낳다 (nahda) with male subject markers or 낣다 variant; Swahili -zaa (same root but male context, e.g., alizaa, akazaa). Distinguished from the female-subject sense by consistent cross-linguistic male-subject framing (engendrar vs dar a luz in Spanish; 'fathered' vs 'bore' in English). Includes Qal perfects, imperfects, participles, and infinitives with masculine subjects.

The passive sense 'to be born,' realized through Qal passive (QalPass) and Niphal stems. Arabic uniformly uses وُلِدَ (wulida, passive of walada) and يُولَدُ (yuuladu, imperfect passive); Korean switches to the entirely different verb 태어나다 (taeeonada) 'to be born' (not 낳다); Swahili uses the passive -zaliwa (e.g., alizaliwa, walizaliwa) — the -w- passive morpheme is a clear discriminator. Spanish uses nacer/nacio (intransitive 'to be born') rather than dar a luz or engendrar. This is a genuine distinct sense confirmed by all six languages using different morphological or lexical strategies from the active senses.

The Hifil causative sense 'to cause to beget, to make bring forth.' Arabic uses أَوْلَدَ (awlada, Form IV causative) in 102052 and أُولِدُ (uulidu) in 102102, and الْمُولِدُ (al-muulidu, causative participle) in 102135 — all distinctly causative morphology (different from the simple وَلَدَ). Korean 낳게 하다 (nahge hada) 'to cause to give birth' with the causative auxiliary; Swahili uses the causative -zalisha (e.g., nisizalishe 102102, ninayezalisha 102135). Distinguished from the simple Qal 'beget' by genuine causative semantics where the subject causes another to give birth. Note: Many Hifil forms of ילד are functionally identical to Qal 'beget/father' and have been merged there; only forms with clear causative semantics are kept here.

The Hofal causative-passive sense meaning 'birth, being born' as a nominalized event. Arabic مِيلَاد (miilad) 'birthday/birth' in 102111 and وِلَادَة (wilaada) 'birth' in 102006 — both nominal/event forms distinct from the simple passive وُلِدَ; Korean 태어난 (taeeonan) 'born' and 태어남 (taeenam) as nominalized form; Swahili kuzaliwa 'to be born' with passive. This captures the Hofal infinitive uses that denote the event or occasion of birth itself rather than a predicate about someone being born.

The Piel intensive/professional sense 'to act as midwife, to assist in childbirth.' Arabic uses the completely different root قَابِلَة (qaabila) 'midwife' from ق-ب-ل 'to receive/accept,' proving this is a lexicalized distinct sense — not merely an inflection of 'bear.' Korean uses the specialized term 산파 (sanpa) 'midwife,' an entirely different lexeme from 낳다. Swahili uses mkunga/wakunga 'midwife(s),' also a completely distinct lexeme from -zaa. The convergence of three unrelated languages all using separate lexemes for this sense (rather than a derived form of 'give birth') confirms it as a genuine distinct meaning. Includes Piel participles (midwife/midwives) and Piel infinitive (the act of midwifing).

The Hitpael reflexive sense 'to register oneself by genealogy, to enroll in a genealogical record.' Arabic فَانْتَسَبُوا (fantasabuu) from the root ن-س-ب (n-s-b) 'lineage/genealogy' — a completely different Semitic root from و-ل-د, proving this is a fully lexicalized distinct sense. Korean 등록하다 (deungnokada) 'to register' — entirely unrelated to birth vocabulary. Swahili -jiandikisha 'to register oneself' — a reflexive form of 'write/record,' again completely unrelated to -zaa. This sense has undergone full semantic shift from the birth domain to the administrative/genealogical domain.

labelChirho: Qal passive participle: the one born / child
descriptionChirho: The substantivized Qal passive participle meaning 'the child, the one born,' used as a noun rather than a verbal predicate. Arabic الْمَوْلُودَ (al-mawluuda) 'the born one/child' — a nominalized participle; Korean 그 아이 (geu ai) 'that child' in 102018, showing full lexicalization as a noun; Swahili uses nominal forms. Distinguished from the predicative passive 'was born' by functioning as a substantive noun referring to the child itself rather than predicating an event of birth.
